title: Rosalind and the Well
premise: August Underhill, a nonbinary urban explorer, has spent twelve years rationalizing the sounds beneath their hometown — until Rosalind, the imaginary friend they buried at age nine, appears on the porch unchanged, warning that something in the unmapped tunnels has learned August's name. As night falls, August discovers that the 'well' is not a place but an invitation: a childhood game played at the edge of the woods that never properly ended, and every person who ever joined owes it a turn. To survive until sunrise, August must choose between protecting the found family who unknowingly re-opened the door and telling them the truth that will make them run — and when dawn finally comes, August learns that loyalty was always the price of admission, and someone must stay below.
about_author: A. M. Amberdale is the pen name of a former municipal surveyor who spent a decade documenting infrastructure that official maps insisted did not exist. They write horror about the places between records, and live somewhere they refuse to put on paper.

chapters.title: The Porch Light
chapters.summary: August's POV. Returning from a tunnel survey that doesn't match any city record, August finds Rosalind — the imaginary friend from childhood, aged nine forever — sitting on the porch steps, patient as furniture. The chapter establishes August's habit of explaining things away, and ends it: for the first time in twelve years, no explanation comes. Beat: dread disguised as nostalgia.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: August's POV, interwoven with flashbacks to age nine. We learn the rules of the old game: knocking on the well cap behind the Henderson property, taking turns 'listening down,' and the day Rosalind stopped being pretend. August catalogs every rational explanation they've built since. Beat: the architecture of denial, and its first hairline crack.

chapters.title: The House That Agreed
chapters.summary: August's POV. Rosalind speaks only in sentences August almost remembers saying. When August tries to photograph him, the images show an empty porch. Inside the house, doors open before August reaches them — the house itself seems to be making room for a guest. Beat: hospitality turned sinister; the home as accomplice.

chapters.title: Found Family
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Priya, August's fellow explorer and de facto roommate, arriving with takeout and survey data. Priya's warmth grounds the book: her banter, her terrible playlists, her blind trust. She notices August is shaken but accepts 'bad day' as an answer. Beat: tenderness established precisely so the reader fears losing it.

chapters.title: What the Survey Didn't Say
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Overlaying August's tunnel measurements on county archives, Priya finds the passages correspond exactly to a structure demolished in 1974: the Henderson well house. Every map since shows nothing there. Someone, or something, has been redrawing reality — or the tunnels were never dug at all. Beat: intellectual horror; the map is lying.

chapters.title: Rosalind Remembers For You
chapters.summary: August's POV. Rosalind begins recounting memories August has suppressed: the fourth child in their childhood friend group, Wren, who 'went down' during the listening game and whose family moved away overnight. Rosalind insists he came back because August called — by mapping the tunnels, August re-said the invitation. Beat: guilt surfaces; curiosity was the summons.

chapters.title: Priya Hears It Too
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Alone in the kitchen at 2 a.m., Priya hears a child counting under the floorboards — patient, unhurried, reaching forty and starting over. She tells herself it's pipes. Then the counting pauses, as if listening back. Beat: the rationalist gets her first unexplainable; solidarity forms in shared fear.

chapters.title: The Rules of the Game
chapters.summary: August's POV. Rosalind lays out the terms: the well grants one listener per generation, chosen by whoever says the words; sunrise ends the night's claims; and anyone who hears their own name spoken from below belongs to it. August realizes Priya said August's name aloud earlier — casually, affectionately — over the open floor vent. Beat: the trap revealed through love.

chapters.title: Down Is a Direction
chapters.summary: August's POV. Against Rosalind's warnings, August enters the storm drain to find the well cap and end the game at its source. The tunnels are wrong — distances fold, August passes the same graffiti three times, each version slightly older. Beat: claustrophobic descent; the explorer's confidence curdles into prey-instinct.

chapters.title: Wren
chapters.summary: August's POV, deep underground. August finds Wren — or what answers to Wren — standing at the well cap, unchanged after thirty years, smiling with too many years of practice. Wren explains the arrangement gently: the well keeps what it's given, but it trades. One name held can buy another released. Beat: horrifying temptation framed as mercy.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Priya, researching the Henderson family in a locked archive room, finds a 1974 newspaper photo: four children at the well, and a fifth figure standing slightly apart, blurred. She recognizes the blur's posture instantly — it's how August stands. Beat: the past and present collapse into one image; dread becomes certainty.

chapters.title: The Name Below
chapters.summary: August's POV. From the well shaft, something speaks August's full name — the deadname August retired years ago, known to no one living. The horror isn't the voice; it's that hearing it feels like being seen completely. August runs. Beat: identity weaponized; the self as vulnerability.

chapters.title: Locks and Lies
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. August returns and lies to Priya — says the tunnels are structurally dangerous, that she should leave town tonight. Priya agrees too easily. Watching her pack, August realizes with cold clarity that the lie protects her only if she believes it, and Priya has never once believed August's explanations. Beat: loyalty vs. truth made literal; the first real fracture.

chapters.title: Rosalind's Confession
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV — the book's only chapter in his voice. He reveals what he is: not an imaginary friend, but the well's negotiator, once a child like Wren, sent up each generation to arrange the trade. He chose to warn August because August, at nine, gave him a name, and names are the one currency the well cannot mint. Beat: sympathy for the monster; love as loophole.

chapters.title: Priya Doesn't Leave
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Twenty miles out of town, Priya turns the car around. She found August's field notes — pages where August's handwriting degrades into a second script, older, looping downward off the page. She won't let August face this alone, even if August lied to make her. Beat: found family chooses itself; the lie fails against loyalty.

chapters.title: The Counting Reaches Forty
chapters.summary: August's POV. Back home, the counting under the floor finishes for the first time in twelve years. Silence follows — worse than the counting. Then every tap in the house runs at once, and the water tastes of iron and pond-bottom. The well has stopped waiting. Beat: the siege begins; stillness as threat.

chapters.title: Holding Out Until Sunrise
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, real-time pressure. August and Priya fortify the house: salt lines from Rosalind's instructions, mirrors facing down, names written and burned. Rosalind stands watch at the threshold, growing fainter with each hour as he spends himself holding the door. The trio becomes, unmistakably, a family under one roof. Beat: warmth inside terror; the calm before the price.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: August's POV. The truth surfaces fully: nine-year-old August, frightened of losing their friends to moving day, spoke the invitation so the group could never scatter — everyone who played would belong to the same place forever. The well took Wren as down payment and waited twelve years for August to come of age and finish paying. Beat: devastating self-reckoning; the child's wish as original sin.

chapters.title: The Trade
chapters.summary: Climax, part one. At the well cap, August offers the only acceptable exchange: themselves, willingly, in place of both Wren and the claim on Priya. Rosalind intervenes, revealing his own name — his true one, pre-Henderson — and spends it voiding the contract's oldest clause. The well takes him instead. Beat: sacrifice; the imaginary friend proves more real than anyone.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: Climax, part two. August and Priya climb out of the collapsing tunnel as the first light hits the tree line, hand in hand, Wren's long-held name finally released behind them. The well house settles into ordinary ruin. August looks back once. Beat: survival earned, not granted; grief and relief in the same breath.

chapters.title: After the Explanation Runs Out
chapters.summary: August's POV, weeks later. August and Priya tell each other everything now — no more explanations, no more protective lies. August stops exploring mapped-adjacent tunnels and starts mapping the ones that are real, leaving the unmapped alone. Some nights, August still sets out a second cup of tea. Beat: mourning integrated; honesty as the new household rule.

chapters.title: The Well Keeps What It's Given
chapters.summary: Final chapter, ambiguous coda. A new family moves into the neighborhood; their daughter mentions a polite boy on the porch who knows all the best hiding places. August, passing on the sidewalk, meets the girl's eyes and says, gently: some friends are only pretend — remember which ones you made up. The last line: somewhere below, patient as furniture, something counts to forty and begins again. Beat: cyclical dread; the story closes its own loop.
